# Fluids with modified spacetime symmetries

Lecture 19 · [Original notes](https://www.alucasphys.com/p7810s2026/p7810s2026_lecture19.pdf)

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives"}
Construct constitutive relations from spatial and time-reversal symmetries; recognize when current and momentum need not coincide; distinguish dissipative transport from Hall transport; calculate the pressure signature of Hall viscosity.
:::

## Which parts of fluid mechanics come from symmetry? {#sec-l19-symmetry}

A gas of structureless particles is nearly isotropic. A suspension of aligned rods, an electron liquid in a crystal, or a chiral active material need not be. Conservation laws survive these changes, but the permitted currents and stresses change. This is a useful test of our understanding: the familiar Navier–Stokes equation is one member of a larger family of hydrodynamic theories.

We retain a conserved scalar density $n$ and momentum density $g_i$, temporarily suppressing energy. Their equations are

$$
\partial_t n+\partial_i J_i=0,\qquad
\partial_t g_i+\partial_j\tau_{ij}=0.
$$ {#eq-l19-conservation}

Let $f(n,\mathbf g)$ be the equilibrium free-energy density and define conjugates $\mu=\partial f/\partial n$ and $v_i=\partial f/\partial g_i$. Here $v_i$ is a thermodynamic variable; without Galilean invariance we must not replace $g_i$ by $mnv_i$ automatically. Likewise, momentum flux $\tau_{ij}$ need not be symmetric if angular momentum can be exchanged with an orientational background.

For generalized time reversal, take an orthogonal matrix $A$ acting on coordinates, with $\mathbf x\mapsto A\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf v\mapsto-A\mathbf v$. Ordinary time reversal has $A=I$. A symmetry combining a reflection with time reversal has a different $A$. The response fields in the stochastic formulation transform along with the physical fields. Requiring the action to change only by a total derivative imposes a local equilibrium identity on ideal currents:

$$
J_j\partial_j\mu+\tau_{ij}\partial_j v_i=\partial_j S_j.
$$ {#eq-l19-potential}

The vector $S_i(\mu,\mathbf v)$ is a constitutive generating function, rather than the entropy density. Comparing independent gradients yields

$$
J_i=\frac{\partial S_i}{\partial\mu},\qquad
\tau_{ij}=\frac{\partial S_j}{\partial v_i}.
$$ {#eq-l19-generated}

This compresses many time-reversal constraints into one symmetry problem: construct every allowed vector $S_i$, then differentiate it. The identity concerns the retained variables and ideal derivative order; including energy requires the corresponding temperature terms.

As a check, an isotropic Galilean fluid has $S_i=P(\mu+mv^2/2)v_i$. Since $\partial P/\partial\mu=n$, differentiation gives $J_i=nv_i$ and $\tau_{ij}=P\delta_{ij}+mnv_iv_j$. Those familiar relations have therefore used both thermodynamics and a boost symmetry.

## Aligned rods: anisotropy without chirality {#sec-l19-rods}

Consider a three-dimensional material invariant under rotations in the $xy$ plane and under $z\mapsto-z$. Let $\lambda_{ij}=\hat z_i\hat z_j$ project along the alignment axis. The director $\hat z_i$ itself changes under the reflection, but $\lambda_{ij}$ does not. Consequently, scalar constitutive functions may depend on $v^2$ and $v_z^2$, and the most general zeroth-order vector is

$$
S_i=F(\mu,v^2,v_z^2)v_i+
H(\mu,v^2,v_z^2)\lambda_{ij}v_j.
$$ {#eq-l19-uniaxial}

There are two directions in which a current can respond to velocity. In particular,

$$
J_i=F_\mu v_i+H_\mu\lambda_{ij}v_j,
$$

while differentiating $S_j$ with respect to $v_i$ produces the pressure-like term $F\delta_{ij}+H\lambda_{ij}$ and velocity-quadratic terms. Mixed tensors $v_i\lambda_{jk}v_k$ and $\lambda_{ik}v_kv_j$ have independent coefficients in general. A stress with $\tau_{xz}\ne\tau_{zx}$ is allowed because the assumed symmetry does not include continuous rotations mixing $x$ and $z$.

At first derivative order, scalar diffusion is governed by

$$
\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_\perp(\delta_{ij}-\lambda_{ij})+
\sigma_\parallel\lambda_{ij}.
$$

Positivity requires $\sigma_\perp,\sigma_\parallel\ge0$. The fourth-rank viscosity tensor is built from $\delta$ and $\lambda$. Before imposing stress symmetry, a useful spanning set is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{ij,kl}={}&\zeta\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}
+a(\delta_{ij}\lambda_{kl}+\lambda_{ij}\delta_{kl})
+b\lambda_{ij}\lambda_{kl}\\
&+c\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}+d\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}
+e\delta_{ik}\lambda_{jl}+f\delta_{jl}\lambda_{ik}\\
&+h(\delta_{il}\lambda_{jk}+\delta_{jk}\lambda_{il}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l19-uniaxial-viscosity}

These are the tensor motifs in the notes, with renamed coefficients. Pair-exchange symmetry $\eta_{ij,kl}=\eta_{kl,ij}$ follows from the relevant Onsager relation. The notes quote further pair identifications in their chosen rotational realization. Such equalities require specifying the angular-momentum/stress assumptions: for example, symmetry of the $xy$ stress forces $c=d$, whereas full three-dimensional stress symmetry constrains the axis-containing terms as well. Ordinary time reversal also prevents a dissipative cross term between the even scalar-density channel and the odd momentum channel in this example. Positivity means $X_{ij}\eta_{ij,kl}X_{kl}\ge0$ for every dissipative gradient $X$. For a projected pair of scalar gradients with quadratic-form matrix $\begin{pmatrix}K_{11}&K_{12}\\K_{12}&K_{22}\end{pmatrix}$, this includes $K_{12}^2\le K_{11}K_{22}$ and nonnegative diagonal entries. These projected entries combine several coefficients in @eq-l19-uniaxial-viscosity; they are not simply the raw coefficients $\zeta,a,b$. One should test the full quadratic form rather than declare each coefficient positive independently.

## A two-dimensional fluid with combined reflection and time reversal {#sec-l19-hall}

Now assume planar rotations and a time reversal combined with $y\mapsto-y$. In two dimensions both $\delta_{ij}$ and the antisymmetric symbol $\epsilon_{ij}$ are available. The trial ideal vector is $S_i=F(\mu,v^2)v_i+H(\mu,v^2)\epsilon_{ij}v_j$. Transforming this expression under the combined symmetry excludes the second term at ideal order. The ideal equations can consequently look ordinary even when derivative corrections are unusual.

For diffusion, the allowed matrix is

$$
\sigma_{ij}=\sigma\delta_{ij}+\sigma_H\epsilon_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-l19-hall-conductivity}

The longitudinal coefficient satisfies $\sigma\ge0$. The Hall coefficient has no sign constraint from entropy production because $a_i\epsilon_{ij}a_j=0$. It rotates a thermodynamic driving force into a perpendicular current. The same algebra explains why it does not contribute to the symmetric noise covariance. “Transport coefficient” therefore does not mean “dissipative coefficient.”

For a symmetric stress, one conventional Hall-viscosity tensor is

$$
\eta^H_{ij,kl}=\frac{\eta_H}{2}
(\epsilon_{ik}\delta_{jl}+\epsilon_{il}\delta_{jk}
+\epsilon_{jk}\delta_{il}+\epsilon_{jl}\delta_{ik}).
$$ {#eq-l19-hall-viscosity}

It is symmetric within each stress pair and antisymmetric under exchanging the two pairs. Thus $X_{ij}\eta^H_{ij,kl}X_{kl}=0$. This is the viscosity counterpart of the preceding Hall conductivity. Numerical factors depend on whether the strain tensor includes a factor $1/2$; @eq-l19-hall-viscosity fixes our convention.

## Supplementary worked example: a transverse pressure drop {#sec-l19-channel}

For constant Hall viscosity and an incompressible two-dimensional fluid, the Hall force can be absorbed into a modified pressure. Choose $\epsilon_{xy}=1$ and vorticity $\omega=\partial_xv_y-\partial_yv_x$. With the corresponding stress convention, the momentum equation takes the form

$$
\rho(\partial_t+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v
=-\nabla(P-\eta_H\omega)+\eta\nabla^2\mathbf v.
$$ {#eq-l19-modified-pressure}

In a channel $0<y<W$, impose no slip and a constant longitudinal gradient $\partial_xP$. The longitudinal solution remains

$$
v_x(y)=\frac{\partial_xP}{2\eta}\,y(y-W),\qquad v_y=0.
$$

However, the transverse equation requires $P-\eta_H\omega$ to be independent of $y$. Since $\omega=-\partial_yv_x$, it follows that

$$
P(W)-P(0)=-\frac{\eta_H}{\eta}\,W\partial_xP.
$$ {#eq-l19-transverse-pressure}

The velocity profile alone cannot reveal $\eta_H$ in this example; a pressure measurement can. Reversing the convention for $\epsilon_{ij}$ reverses both $\eta_H$ and the displayed sign, leaving the physical prediction unchanged. Spatial variation of $\eta_H$, compressibility, and boundary traction can prevent this simple pressure absorption.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfalls"}
Anisotropy does not by itself imply dissipation. Onsager constraints involve the actual time-reversal operation, including any reflection. A Hall coefficient need not be positive. Finally, a nonsymmetric momentum flux needs an angular-momentum accounting; it cannot be inserted into an otherwise rotationally invariant isolated fluid without explanation.
:::

## Exercises and solutions {#sec-l19-exercises}

1. Differentiate $S_j$ in @eq-l19-uniaxial with respect to $v_i$ and identify a term that can make $\tau_{ij}$ nonsymmetric.
2. Prove directly that a Hall conductivity cannot produce local entropy proportional to $\nabla\mu\cdot\mathbf J$.
3. In the channel example, find the vorticity at each wall and explain why the two wall pressures differ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
1. The terms $2F_{v_z^2}v_j\lambda_{ik}v_k$ and $2H_{v^2}\lambda_{jk}v_kv_i$ are transposes with unrelated coefficients. They need not cancel in $\tau_{ij}-\tau_{ji}$.
2. The Hall contribution is proportional to $(\partial_i\mu)\epsilon_{ij}(\partial_j\mu)$, which equals its own negative after relabeling $i,j$ and therefore vanishes.
3. $\omega(0)=\partial_xP\,W/(2\eta)$ and $\omega(W)=-\partial_xP\,W/(2\eta)$. The constant transverse modified pressure gives @eq-l19-transverse-pressure.
:::
